newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Zuma gives some ground in medicines row.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Zuma gives some ground in medicines row.

text.p: South African Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma said on Thursday she had removed a clause from proposed drugs legislation that would have barred the sale of branded medicines to the state.
She said a clause that "no person shall sell any medicine to the state if the brand name of that medicine appears on its label" had been removed from the bill.

But she told a news conference on changes to the Medicines and Related Substances Control Amendment Bill that parallel imports of drugs would go ahead, although under tighter guidelines than previously planned.
"The main principles remain. These (include) generic substitution to reduce costs (and) parallel importation," she said.
Zuma added that the bill had been amended to ensure "parallel importation will be done under clearly defined conditions and registrations".
The proposed legislation has now been approved by South Africa's cabinet and will go back to parliament for debate, Zuma said.
Zuma has been locked in an at times bitter dispute with the pharmacueitcals industry over her planned reforms, which she sees as vital if the cost of the country's health bill is to be reduced.
"Of course the pharmaceutical manufacturers don't like it, and we didn't expect them to like it because it will affect their profits...we have to strike a balance.
"While they make their profits, we must be able to save lives, even the poor ones," Zuma said.

Malcolm Jones, a director in the health department, told the news conference that parallel imports were necessary because some drugs were far more expensive in South Africa than they were in other countries.

Currently, drugs that are registered by a South African manufacturer are bought from that manufacturer. Under the new system, the South African government would buy a drug in another country if it was cheaper there.

The latest changes to the plans are the second time Zuma has sought to make concessions to the drugs industry after she backed down last year in the face of a legal challenge from SmithKline Beecham Plc.
The pharmaceutical manufacturers' industry argues Zuma is hurting its right to free trade.
It is particularly aggrieved at plans to insist pharmacists substitute brand-name drugs with cheaper generic equivalents.
The industry says it is willing to compete with generics on a level playing field, but that there should not be any mandatory replacements.

The scrapping of the plans to limit the use of brand names will be welcomed by drugs firms, especially in the United States, which had threatened to take South Africa to the World Trade Organisation on the grounds of infringing intellectual property rights.
Other overseas firms said the moves threatened plans to invest in South Africa.
